title: The Script Tax: Measuring Tokenization-Driven Efficiency and Latency Disparities in Multilingual Language Models
problem_statement: Pretrained multilingual language models are often assumed to be script-agnostic, yet subword tokenizers can impose systematic computational, latency, and information-cost disparities on specific writing systems. When a tokenizer segments one orthography into substantially more subword fragments than another orthography representing identical linguistic content, the resulting sequence inflation increases memory consumption and inference latency while degrading modeling efficiency. Furthermore, standard token-level negative log-likelihood metrics fail to detect this inefficiency because predicting small subword units artificially lowers per-token loss.
domain: Natural Language Processing (NLP), Multilingual Language Models, Tokenization Efficiency and Fairness, Subword Fragmentation, Inference Latency
theoretical_framework: The conceptual framework of the script tax operationalizes tokenization disparities along three interrelated dimensions: tokenization fragmentation (measured by word fertility), inference computational overhead (governed by superlinear Transformer attention scaling relative to sequence length), and character-normalized information cost (measured via Bits Per Character to resolve the subword fragmentation negative log-likelihood paradox).
methodology: The authors established a controlled paired evaluation framework comparing matched sentence pairs with identical linguistic content across two orthographic variants (Orthography A and Orthography B) using two multilingual masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R). The methodology quantifies the script tax across three primary axes: (1) tokenization fragmentation measured through token fertility (tokens per word) and fertility differences; (2) information efficiency measured through Bits Per Character (BPC), which normalizes masked-token loss by Unicode character count rather than subword token count; and (3) computational overhead measured through median inference latency and throughput on identical hardware. Additionally, the authors implemented a round-trip Character Error Rate (CER) check using bidirectional orthographic mapping functions to verify that measured performance differences originate from tokenizer mechanics rather than transliteration noise.
datasets: Paired parallel sentence corpus consisting of matched sentence pairs (D = {(x_A^(n), x_B^(n))}_{n=1}^N) expressing identical linguistic content across two orthographic variants (higher-fragmentation Orthography B versus lower-fragmentation Orthography A)

metrics: Bits Per Character (BPC, character-normalized loss in bits)

key_findings: Pretrained multilingual language models exhibit substantial tokenization fragmentation disparities across orthographic variants with identical linguistic content, resulting in a ~3.4x fertility increase (6.73 to 6.85 tokens/word versus 2.10 to 2.35 tokens/word).
Subword sequence inflation induces a 16.5x inference slowdown on identical hardware, reducing throughput from ~3.8 sentences/second to ~0.23 sentences/second due to superlinear attention scaling.

Character-normalized information cost (BPC) degrades substantially for the higher-fragmentation orthography (+19.7% for mBERT and +47.1% for XLM-R), demonstrating that token-level loss metrics conceal genuine representational inefficiency.
Round-trip Character Error Rate evaluation (CER_rt = 0.31) demonstrates that the observed performance gaps reflect tokenizer-induced processing behavior rather than dataset conversion noise.

Pretrained subword tokenizers create structural inequities in computational accessibility and representation quality across writing systems, demonstrating that tokenization choices directly govern multilingual model fairness.
scope_and_delimitations: Model scope is delimited to two multilingual masked language models: mBERT and XLM-R.
Linguistic evaluation is delimited to two orthographic variants expressing identical content within a paired sentence setup.
Experimental hardware evaluation is delimited to a single fixed hardware and inference configuration.

Evaluation scope is delimited to tokenization fertility, character-normalized masked language modeling loss (BPC), and inference latency, excluding downstream fine-tuning tasks and autoregressive generation.

limitations.verbatim_excerpt: Our analysis is limited to two orthographic variants and two multilingual masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R), so the magnitude of the script tax may differ for other scripts, tokenizers, and model families. The paired setup relies on an orthography conversion pipeline; while round-trip CER (CERrt) offers a robustness check, residual conversion artifacts may still influence results. Finally, latency numbers depend on a specific hardware/inference configuration, though the relative penalties from sequence inflation should generalize qualitatively.
limitations.summary: The authors identify three primary limitations: the study examines only two orthographic variants and two masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R), which may not capture the magnitude of disparities in other scripts or model families; the paired experimental design depends on an automated orthography conversion pipeline where residual conversion artifacts could affect results despite round-trip validation; and exact latency measurements depend on a specific hardware configuration, although relative performance penalties generalize qualitatively.

generalizability_gap: The study evaluates only two orthographic variants and two encoder-only masked language models (mBERT and XLM-R), leaving unexamined autoregressive decoder-only architectures (modern generative LLMs), broader non-Latin scripts, and alternative hardware acceleration environments.
methodological_gap: The evaluation relies on an orthographic conversion pipeline that exhibits imperfect round-trip reconstruction (CER_rt = 0.31), omits downstream task benchmarks (such as classification, question answering, or machine translation), and does not directly measure memory bandwidth or energy consumption during inference.
future_work: Extending script tax measurements to broader writing systems, diverse tokenizer architectures, and autoregressive large language model families.
Designing script-aware tokenization interventions, including vocabulary augmentation, dynamic re-tokenization, and script-balanced pretraining.
Incorporating character-normalized loss metrics (BPC) and compute-aware latency metrics into standard multilingual NLP benchmark evaluations.
Refining bidirectional orthographic conversion pipelines to eliminate residual conversion noise in paired cross-script analyses.
